chapter: Dancing schools, Sapiro and Jelly Roll Morton
title: Discovering Jelly Roll Morton's music; the Red Hot Pepper Stomp record
summary: Morton's name meant little to him at first; as he learned the older musicians' stories he realized Morton had something. He kept a record he made with Morton in 1928 and explains why dancing schools used stock arrangements.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: Now, when you worked with Jelly Roll, was he already a name known to you when you went in?

No. Not really. I'd probably heard his name, but he didn't -- I mean the name didn't mean too much to me at that time. I was just discovering all these people and this music, I just discovered, you know, what it meant and what they were playing, because at that time I was more steeped in what was happening right here in New York, and as I discovered these people -- you know, like it was -- mostly what happened was, you know, like you say, the musicians' club, you know, all these older musicians, they sit around and talk like about Chicago and wherever, and I listened, and like they used to talk about Joe Oliver and Johnny St.Cyr. and all those old guys, you know --
Well, they weren't really that old then.
They weren't really that old then.

Well, they were older than I was, you know. I don't know how old -- I was about 17, 18, 19. They were probably 25. I called them old, you know. Yeah. So anyway, when I discovered Jelly Roll, you know, he -- I realized that he really had something, you know, his style and his music and his -- and I have one record home now I made with Jelly Roll. I was just playing it last week. I made it in must have been '28, '28 when I --
Well, I can't imagine Jelly Roll playing stock arrangements.

Well, in the dancing school, see, in the dancing school you played so much you had to play stock arrangements. See, you played -- the schedule in most dancing schools was you played 50 minutes and would rest 10, or 55 minutes and rest 5. You know, because if you had to get off the bandstand you just got off. Or if you wanted a sandwich, you just got off and got your sandwich, you know, or something like that, but the music was continuous, continuous, so of course you couldn't have special arrangements like that. And you played stock arrangements, stock arrangements, and --
